title: The handkerchief bra
hook: A 19-year-old made a bra from two silk handkerchiefs and patented it.
peek: Getting ready for a dance in 1913, Mary Phelps Jacob found her corset spoiled the line of a sheer gown. With a maid's help she pinned two handkerchiefs and some ribbon into something softer, then patented it in 1914.
lede: In 1913 Mary Phelps Jacob, a 19-year-old New York debutante, was dressing for a ball in a sheer evening gown. Her stiff whalebone corset poked out at the neckline. So she and her maid stitched together two silk handkerchiefs and a length of pink ribbon. Friends asked for copies, and in November 1914 she was granted a patent for a "backless brassiere".

bullets.text: Her design was light and soft, sat flat under thin fabric and separated the breasts rather than pressing them into one shape like a corset. The patent described it as suited to both evening wear and daily use.

Jacob made a few hundred by hand but found running a business tiresome. She sold the patent to the Warner Brothers Corset Company for $1,500. Warner is often said to have earned millions from bras in the decades that followed.

She did not invent the idea outright. Inventors had patented breast supports in the 1800s, and other bra-like garments were on sale. Her version is remembered because it was the first to be patented under the name brassiere and sold widely.
Jacob later took the name Caresse Crosby. In Paris in the 1920s she and her husband Harry ran the Black Sun Press, which printed early editions of writers including James Joyce and Ernest Hemingway.
